content:
Yesterday we read about the men who were unclean and could not keep the Passover at the right time. They came to Moses and asked; and God gave them a way. He said: if anyone is unclean because of a dead body, or if they are on a journey far from home, they can still keep the Passover. They just need to do it one month later, on the fourteenth day of the second month. But God also made it clear that this mercy had a limit. If someone was clean, if they were at home, if there was nothing stopping them; and they still did not keep the Passover; they would be cut off from the community. To miss it without reason was to say, in effect: this does not matter to me. And Yahweh took that seriously.

So the rule was simple. A genuine reason; uncleanness, a long journey, and God made a way. One month later, the door was still open. But careless neglect, with no excuse, that was a different matter entirely. God is full of grace, but His grace is not for those who do not want it. It is for those who are hungry, those who are hindered, those who are far away but still reaching toward Him.

Yesterday we ended with a question: why did God say one month later?
Why not two months? Why not wait until the person was clean and then let them come at any time? Why was the second Passover placed exactly thirty days after the first? At first it seems like a practical answer; just give them a reasonable amount of time. But when we look at what happened in Israel's history at exactly that one-month mark, we see that God was saying something far deeper than a simple rule.

Israel left Egypt on the fifteenth day of the first month. Thirty days later; exactly one month after the Exodus, the whole congregation came into the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai. We read this in Exodus 16:1. And it was right there, at that one-month point, that the people ran out of food.

They were hungry. They complained. And God answered. Exodus 16:4 tells us what He said: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you." That was the first time the manna fell. The very first time God sent bread from heaven was exactly one month after Israel left Egypt; around the same moment that God had marked as the window for the Second Passover.

This is not a coincidence. When we see things like this in Scripture; where the timing lines up too precisely to be accidental, it is because God placed them there deliberately. The Second Passover window and the first day of the manna land on closely the same point in time, Nisan 14th and 15th. And that tells us something. Yahweh was connecting two things: the mercy for those who missed the lamb, and the bread that came down from heaven for the hungry. The one who was shut out of the first Passover was the same kind of person who showed up starving in that wilderness. And at that exact moment; God rained down bread.

When we come to the New Testament, Christ himself draws this connection clearly. In John 6, the people in the crowd mention that Moses gave their fathers bread in the wilderness; the manna. Christ answers them and says: Moses did not give that bread. My Father gave it. And then he says something remarkable: "I am the bread of life. He that comes to me shall never hunger, and he that believes on me shall never thirst" (John 6:35). Christ is saying plainly: I am what the manna was pointing to all along. The bread that rained down in the wilderness was a picture of me.

So now the picture in Numbers 9 becomes full. The Second Passover was given for the person who was unclean, the person who was far from home, the person who had missed the appointed time through no fault of their own. And at that exact moment in history; one month after the Exodus, the very window of the Second Passover, the true bread from heaven appeared in the wilderness.
Not for the priests only. Not for the elders only. Not for the ceremonially clean only. For everyone. Every person in the camp was fed. No one was excluded.

This takes us to a deeper truth that God was quietly building into the story of Israel. The first Passover was the foundation of the old covenant; the Law given through Moses, the first administration of God's plan for His people. It had its appointed times, its requirements of cleanness, its conditions. If you were unclean, you could not come. If you missed the time, you were shut out.
The Law was holy and good, but it had limits. Not everyone could meet its conditions. And over time, under that first covenant, man became unclean, man wandered, man failed to keep the appointed time.

But God never intended to leave people in that place. The Second Passover provision in Numbers 9 was God's quiet signal, placed in the Law itself, that a second covenant was coming. The first was not the final. There would be a second window; and when that second window opened, the bread of heaven would not come with conditions of cleanness or requirements of distance.
It would simply fall. Freely. For everyone who was hungry.

That second window is the New Covenant through Christ. The true Passover Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. The manna who came down from heaven not for one nation and not for the ceremonially clean, but for all who are hungry. Under the Law, missing the Passover without reason meant being cut off. But under the New Covenant, the door is wide open to the unclean,
to the wanderer, to the one who has been far away. Christ himself said it with no conditions attached: "He that comes to me I will in no wise cast out"
(John 6:37). No cleanness requirement. No appointed month. No second deadline. Whoever comes; will be fed.

The Second Passover provision teaches us something about the character of God that we must hold onto. He is holy; and He takes His covenant seriously. The person who ignored the Passover with no excuse was cut off. Yahweh does not treat His covenant as optional. But at the same time, He is full of mercy; and He looks at the person who is genuinely hindered, genuinely far away, genuinely struggling with their uncleanness, and He says: there is still a way. Come one month later. The lamb will still be there.

God never closes a door without opening a window of grace. The manna did not fall on a palace. It fell in a wilderness, on hungry wanderers who had nothing. And Christ, the true manna, still comes today in exactly the same way. Not to the comfortable. Not to those who have everything sorted. He comes to the soul that is unclean and knows it. He comes to the one who is far from home. He comes to the one who missed every appointment and somehow still finds themselves hungry and reaching. For that person, the Second Passover provision says: the door is not shut. Come and eat. The bread from heaven is still falling. But wait, there is one more information in this, God gave this 2nd Passover only to the ones who are ceremonially unclean & those who are away on a trip and we shall study about this in our tomorrow’s Morning light.

title: Prayer
text:
**O give thanks unto Yahweh, for He is good; for His mercy endures forever. Psalm 107:1**

O God, our Father,

We thank You that You are not a God who simply shuts doors.

You built a second window into the Law itself,

long before the New Covenant was proclaimed;

because You already knew that people would be unclean,

that they would wander, that they would miss the appointed time.

And right at that second window, You rained bread from heaven.

We are those wanderers. We are the hungry ones in the wilderness.

And Christ, the true manna, came for us.

Let us never take that lightly. Let us never drift into careless neglect;

for we have seen what happens to those who had no excuse and still would not come.

Keep us hungry. Keep us reaching. Keep us grateful that the door is still open.

We ask this in the name of our Passover Lamb and living Bread, Christ our Messiah.

Amen.
